obliterate

uh-BLIT-er-ayt -- from Latin ob- ('against, over') + littera ('letter'): literally 'to strike out the letters.' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To obliterate is to destroy something so completely that no trace of it remains.

The renovation crew's sledgehammers obliterated the last standing wall of the old gymnasium within an hour.

Example

Restorers examining the old fresco found that centuries of candle smoke and flaking plaster had obliterated the original mural's colors and lines -- not even a faint outline survived.

When something is destroyed so thoroughly that no trace of it remains at all, it has been obliterated -- notice this is about erasing a thing or a mark, not defeating a living opponent (that's annihilate, taught later in this unit).

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

demolish: To demolish is to deliberately knock down a structure -- a bridge, a factory, a condemned house -- usually with the rubble hauled off afterward. To obliterate goes beyond knocking down: it erases something so totally that no trace of it is left anywhere.

delete: Delete is the everyday word for removing something stored -- a file, a photo, a sentence -- and a deleted thing can often be recovered from a backup. To obliterate is to remove beyond any recovery, leaving nothing that shows the thing ever existed.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

preserve: to keep something safe from harm or loss

safeguard: to protect something from harm or damage

Where it sits · how completely every trace is removed

erase → obliterate → expunge

erase vs. obliterate: Erase is a simple, everyday word, often literal -- erasing a pencil mark or a word on a whiteboard. Obliterate is far stronger, used for large-scale, total destruction that leaves nothing behind at all.

expunge vs. obliterate: Expunge is at least as strong as obliterate and more final in one arena: the official record. When a court expunges a conviction, the entry is treated as never having existed -- removed not just from sight but from the books.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ob-: against, over (Latin)

root — -liter-: letter (Latin (littera))

suffix — -ate: to make or do; forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together: Latin ob- ('against, over') plus littera ('letter') plus the verb suffix -ate: literally 'to strike over the letters' until they cannot be read. That is why obliterate means to erase or destroy without a trace.

Use the root in a new word: literacy: The volunteer program focuses on adult literacy, teaching people to read and write for the first time.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Obliterate typically describes erasing a thing, mark, or trace so completely that nothing is left -- contrast this with annihilate, taught later in this same unit, which usually describes utterly defeating a living opponent or organized group rather than erasing a trace.
